questions.q: Res Judicata is defined under which section of the Code of Civil Procedure?
o: Section 9
Section 10
Section 11
Section 15
questions.src: Section 11 CPC codifies the doctrine of Res Judicata.

questions.q: Which section of CPC provides that civil courts have jurisdiction to try all civil suits unless barred?
o: Section 8
Section 9
Section 12
Section 15
questions.src: Section 9 establishes the general jurisdiction of civil courts, subject to express/implied bars.

questions.q: "Res Sub Judice" under Section 10 CPC applies when:
o: An earlier suit on the same matter has ALREADY been decided
An earlier suit on the same matter, between the same parties, is still PENDING in a competent court
No earlier suit ever existed
Only in criminal proceedings
questions.src: Res Sub Judice (S.10) concerns a PENDING earlier suit, distinct from Res Judicata (S.11) which concerns an already-DECIDED matter.

questions.q: The Latin maxim "interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium" is most directly associated with which CPC doctrine?
o: Res Sub Judice
Res Judicata
Set-off
Counterclaim
questions.src: This maxim ("it is in the interest of the state that there be an end to litigation") underlies the doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11.

questions.q: Under Section 20 CPC, a suit may generally be instituted in a court within whose jurisdiction:
o: Only the plaintiff resides
The defendant resides/carries on business, OR the cause of action wholly or partly arises
Only the subject property is situated, in every type of suit
Only the High Court decides
questions.src: Section 20 provides the general rule for place of suing, based on defendant's location or where the cause of action arose.

questions.q: Under Section 80 CPC, a suit against the Government generally cannot be instituted until:
o: One month after filing a complaint
The EXPIRATION OF TWO MONTHS after delivering a written notice
Immediately, with no waiting period
Five years after the cause of action arose
questions.src: Section 80 mandates a two-month notice period before suing the Government or a public officer for official acts.

questions.q: Under Order II Rule 2 CPC, if a plaintiff omits to sue for one of several reliefs arising from the same cause of action, they:
o: May always file a fresh suit for the omitted relief later without restriction
Are generally BARRED from a later separate suit for the omitted relief, unless leave of court was obtained
Must always include every possible relief or lose the entire suit
Can only proceed if the defendant consents
questions.src: Order II Rule 2 requires a plaintiff to include their whole claim in one suit, barring most later separate suits for omitted reliefs.

questions.q: Pleadings, under Order VI CPC, must state:
o: The detailed evidence supporting each claim
MATERIAL FACTS, not the evidence by which those facts are to be proved
Only legal citations, no facts
Nothing specific, format is unrestricted
questions.src: The fundamental rule of pleading requires stating material facts, leaving evidence for the trial stage.

questions.q: Which Order and Rule of CPC governs the AMENDMENT of pleadings?
o: Order 5
Order 6 Rule 17
Order 7
Order 8
questions.src: Order VI Rule 17 governs amendment of pleadings, allowing courts to permit changes necessary for determining the real questions in controversy.

questions.q: When deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11 (rejection of plaint), a court may examine:
o: Both the plaint and the defendant's written statement equally
ONLY the averments made in the plaint itself (and documents filed with it)
Only oral evidence presented at trial
Only the opinion of the opposing counsel
questions.src: A classic AIBE trap -- Order VII Rule 11 applications are decided based on the plaint alone, not the defence.

questions.q: In Srihari Hanumandas Totala v. Hemant Vithal Kamat (2021), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata:
o: Can always be decided through a simple Order VII Rule 11 application
CANNOT be invoked as a ground for rejecting a plaint under Order VII Rule 11(d), since it requires examining the earlier suit's full record
Does not exist as a valid legal doctrine
Applies only to criminal cases
questions.src: This modern ruling clarified that Res Judicata's complexity exceeds what a bare Rule 11 rejection application can properly resolve.

questions.q: If a written statement is not filed within the prescribed time, under Order VIII Rule 10, the court:
o: Must automatically dismiss the entire suit
MAY pronounce judgment or pass such order as it deems fit
Has no power to act at all
Must wait indefinitely for the written statement
questions.src: Order VIII Rule 10 gives the court discretion to act, including potentially proceeding to judgment, if the written statement is not timely filed.

questions.q: "Set-Off," under Order VIII Rule 6 CPC, allows a defendant to:
o: Raise an entirely unrelated independent claim against the plaintiff
Claim a MONEY debt owed by the plaintiff be adjusted against the plaintiff's claim in the SAME suit
File a completely separate, new lawsuit only
Demand the case be transferred to a different court
questions.src: Set-off specifically involves a money claim being adjusted against the plaintiff's claim within the existing suit.

questions.q: A "Counterclaim," as distinguished from a "Set-off," allows a defendant to:
o: Only claim money debts owed by the plaintiff
Raise their OWN independent claim against the plaintiff, even if UNRELATED to the plaintiff's original claim
Never raise any claim of their own
Only be used in criminal proceedings
questions.src: Counterclaims are broader than set-off, allowing genuinely independent claims regardless of connection to the plaintiff's suit.

questions.q: If the PLAINTIFF fails to appear when the suit is called for hearing (under Order IX), the court may generally:
o: Automatically rule in the plaintiff's favour
DISMISS the suit
Adjourn indefinitely with no consequence
Transfer the case to a criminal court
questions.src: Plaintiff non-appearance under Order IX can result in dismissal of the suit.

questions.q: If the DEFENDANT fails to appear while the plaintiff is present (under Order IX), the court may:
o: Automatically dismiss the plaintiff's suit
Proceed EX PARTE, deciding the case without hearing the defendant
Postpone the case for one year automatically
Refer the matter to arbitration compulsorily
questions.src: Defendant non-appearance can lead to an ex parte decree, decided without the defendant's participation.

questions.q: Under Order XXXIX (Temporary Injunctions), courts typically examine which THREE factors?
o: Only the financial status of the parties
Prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury
Only the age of the dispute
Only whether the parties are related
questions.src: These three classic factors form the standard test courts apply when deciding whether to grant a temporary injunction.

questions.q: For breach of a temporary injunction under Order 39, the maximum period of detention in civil prison is:
o: 1 month
3 months
1 year
5 years
questions.src: Order 39 Rule 2A prescribes a maximum civil prison detention period of 3 months for breach of an injunction order.

questions.q: For breach of a temporary injunction, the maximum VALIDITY of an attachment order (absent extension) is:
o: 3 months
6 months
1 year
5 years
questions.src: The maximum validity period for such an attachment order is generally 1 year, unless extended by the court for good reason.

questions.q: Section 89 CPC provides for reference of a suit, where settlement elements exist, to:
o: Only the Supreme Court directly
Arbitration, Conciliation, Judicial Settlement (including Lok Adalat), or Mediation
Only criminal courts
No alternative mechanism exists under CPC
questions.src: Section 89 connects CPC directly to the broader ADR framework, offering multiple alternative dispute resolution pathways.

questions.q: Order XXI CPC, one of the longest and most detailed Orders, primarily governs:
o: Filing of the initial plaint
EXECUTION of decrees -- how a decree-holder actually obtains what the court awarded
Framing of issues only
Appointment of judges
questions.src: Order XXI covers the practical mechanics of decree execution, including attachment, sale, and delivery of property.

questions.q: A "Second Appeal" (Sections 100-103 CPC), unlike a First Appeal, may generally be filed only on the ground of:
o: Any factual dispute whatsoever
A SUBSTANTIAL QUESTION OF LAW
The amount of money involved
The personal preference of the parties
questions.src: Second Appeal is deliberately restricted to substantial questions of law, distinguishing it from the broader First Appeal.

questions.q: "Revision" under Section 115 CPC refers to:
o: A right of appeal available to any party automatically
The High Court's SUPERVISORY power over subordinate courts acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
A power exercised only by the Supreme Court
An automatic re-trial of every case
questions.src: Revision is a supervisory jurisdiction, distinct from an ordinary right of appeal, focused on jurisdictional errors.

questions.q: "Review" under Section 114 and Order XLVII CPC is decided by:
o: A higher appellate court only
The SAME court that passed the original decree/order, on specified narrow grounds
Only the Supreme Court
A newly constituted special tribunal
questions.src: Review is distinctive in being heard by the SAME court, unlike appeal (a different, higher court) or revision (a supervisory court).

questions.q: In Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorjin Debi (1960), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata:
o: Only applies between two entirely separate lawsuits, never within one case
Applies not only to separate suits but also to DIFFERENT STAGES of the SAME proceeding
Does not apply to civil matters at all
Was abolished by this very judgment
questions.src: This case extended Res Judicata's application to different stages within a single ongoing proceeding, not merely separate suits.

questions.q: In Mathura Prasad v. Dossabhoi N.B. Jeejeebhoy (1970), the Supreme Court held that Res Judicata applies to:
o: Pure questions of law only, never facts
Issues of FACT, not to pure questions of LAW decided in an earlier proceeding
Neither facts nor law
Only criminal matters
questions.src: This case clarified an important limit on Res Judicata's scope -- it operates on factual issues, not pure legal questions.

questions.q: A civil suit contesting a right to property or a public office is considered a suit of a "civil nature" under Section 9, EVEN IF:
o: The right depends entirely on questions of religious rites or ceremonies
The parties are government officials
The property value exceeds a certain threshold
The suit is filed after a specified deadline
questions.src: Explanation I to Section 9 specifically confirms this remains a suit of civil nature despite the religious-rites dependency.

questions.q: For IMMOVABLE property specifically, under Section 16 CPC, a suit must generally be filed:
o: Wherever the plaintiff happens to reside
In the court within whose jurisdiction the property is SITUATED
Only in the High Court of the relevant state
Only in Delhi, regardless of property location
questions.src: Section 16 establishes situs-based jurisdiction specifically for suits relating to immovable property.

questions.q: A general or evasive denial in a Written Statement, where specific facts are not clearly addressed, may be treated by the court as:
o: An automatic dismissal of the entire suit
An ADMISSION of the corresponding allegation
Irrelevant to the proceedings
Grounds for the plaintiff to be penalised
questions.src: Order VIII's pleading rules mean vague or evasive denials risk being construed as admissions of the plaintiff's allegations.

questions.q: Under Order XL CPC, a court may appoint a Receiver where it appears:
o: Never, this power does not exist under CPC
JUST AND CONVENIENT to preserve/manage disputed property during litigation
Only after the final decree is passed
Only in criminal proceedings
questions.src: Order XL empowers courts to appoint a Receiver as another form of interim protective relief, distinct from a temporary injunction.
